## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

_How can a carefully selected subset retain most of the value of a much larger dataset?_

Training pays to acquire, label, score, move, and process examples even though their learning value differs. Large datasets contain redundant, noisy, or target-misaligned samples, while scarce regions may lack the cases a model needs, such as the rare conditions under which a deployed system is most likely to fail. Training on every example treats a near-duplicate and a rare failure case as equally worth paying for, and at scale much of the compute budget can go to relearning what the model already knows. That heterogeneity turns the choice of examples into a systems optimization rather than a data-cleaning chore. The objective is therefore not the smallest dataset but the lowest end-to-end cost of reaching target quality without losing rare cases, underrepresented groups, or deployment-relevant coverage. Every strategy adds its own overhead: examples must be scored, generated, shuffled, stored, or validated, and those costs can erase the savings they promise. That judgment must be made end to end, because gains in labeling or training can be erased by selection latency, storage access, or distributed coordination. A method is worth applying only when the learning it preserves or creates exceeds the work required to apply it. This distinction matters across repeated experiments, where useful reductions compound, and across adaptation, where the value of an example changes with the model and target distribution. In D·A·M terms, it is data-algorithm co-design: shape the training signal so each unit of machine work yields more useful learning.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Explain data selection as data-algorithm co-design that controls sample value, training work, and labeling cost
- Calculate the information-compute ratio and apply the compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter check to diagnose a data-starved run
- Apply the selection inequality to test whether selection overhead beats full-dataset training cost
- Compare deduplication, coreset selection, and quality pruning for reducing redundant pretraining data
- Design curriculum, active learning, synthetic-data, or label-free strategies for changing data value during training
- Evaluate whether a selection pipeline keeps the accelerator fed under storage locality, data echoing, and multi-accelerator consistency constraints
- Select data-selection investments using return on investment, break-even, and amortization analysis

:::

## The Data Wall {#sec-data-selection-data-selection-fundamentals-e839}

The **data wall**\index{Data wall!definition} is the point at which the compute available for training grows faster than the supply of novel, high-quality examples to spend it on.[^fn-data-wall-scaling] Every example a training run processes costs the same forward pass, backward pass, and optimizer update, whether it teaches the model something new or repeats what the model already knows. A duplicated image, a mislabeled record, and a rare boundary case cost the same arithmetic but do not contribute the same learning signal. @Sec-model-training made each of those steps as cheap as one machine allows and accounted for a whole run as roughly $6\Parameters\DatasetSize$ floating-point operations for $\Parameters$ parameters and $\DatasetSize$ tokens. Once each step is cheap, the next saving lies upstream, in which examples deserve a step at all. @Sec-model-training costed a full GPT-2 XL run on one H100; this chapter asks how many of those steps were worth taking.

::: {.column-margin}
```{=latex}
\vspace*{-18mm}
```
![](images/svg/data_selection_scaling_saturation.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two trend lines labeled compute and data diverge, opening a red-shaded gap labeled wall."}

*Compute outruns high-quality data supply; the widening gap is the data wall.*
:::

Increasing the amount of training data has long been a standard way to improve models. Scaling laws\index{Scaling laws!data-compute asymmetry}[^fn-scaling-laws-origin] [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022chinchilla] quantify how model performance can improve with dataset size, and teams have responded by collecting and generating more examples. Accelerator fleets, however, can expand usable compute faster than the supply of novel, high-quality human-generated text and images. Much of the easily accessible public web has already been incorporated into large training corpora, and expert labeling capacity grows slowly. This asymmetry shifts engineering focus from indiscriminate data ingestion toward maximizing the learning signal extracted from every stored and processed sample.

[^fn-scaling-laws-origin]: **Scaling laws**\index{Scaling laws!power-law origin}: Jared Kaplan and colleagues at Johns Hopkins and OpenAI empirically demonstrated in 2020 that language model loss follows power-law relationships with model size, dataset size, and compute budget over the regimes they studied [@kaplan2020scaling]. Their fitted data exponent was approximately $\Glyph{\alpha} = 0.095$ in $\LossFunction \propto \DataScalingLossFactor$. The value is not universal, but the diminishing-return shape makes it possible to reason about when selection becomes more cost-effective than collection.

[^fn-data-wall-scaling]: **Data wall**\index{Data wall!scaling constraint}: Unlike compute (which scales with capital expenditure) or algorithms (which improve through research), the stock of high-quality human-generated text grows slowly; Epoch AI's updated projections estimated that, under the paper's modeled consumption assumptions, models could use datasets roughly equal in size to the stock of public human-generated text between 2026 and 2032 [@villalobos2024will]. The point for systems design is not a fixed calendar deadline; it is that data can become a supply constraint rather than merely an economic one. The wall does not change how many operations $(\Operations)$ a run performs. It lowers the learning each of those operations yields, because once quality data runs short, additional compute spent on repeated or weaker data yields diminishing accuracy regardless of hardware throughput.

Scaling dataset size eventually encounters the finite stock of high-quality human speech and text. @Sec-data-engineering measured that climb, and @fig-running-out-of-human-data sets the largest training corpora against the estimated stock of public text, between $10^{14}$ and $10^{15}$ tokens, which they reach late this decade at the fitted rate. That is the wall at frontier scale, on fleets far larger than one machine.

GPT-2 XL\index{GPT-2!data selection} shows the same wall on one machine. The arithmetic needs only the corpus size, the token budget of the original run, and the fitted compute-optimal balance between parameters and tokens.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ GPT-2, the bandwidth-bound lighthouse for decoder-only language models, is established in @sec-network-architectures-inference-memory-bandwidth-wall-98d1.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: gpt2-data-wall-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ GPT-2 XL DATA WALL ON ONE MACHINE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: GPT-2 data-wall paragraph in
# │          @sec-data-selection-data-selection-fundamentals-e839; reused in
# │          @sec-data-selection-computeoptimal-frontier-24ba, the deduplication
# │          estimate in @sec-data-selection-data-deduplication-6c20, and the
# │          budget-only pitfall in @sec-data-selection-fallacies-pitfalls-f4d0.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that one eight-accelerator machine outruns GPT-2's corpus.
# │ Show:    Unique WebText tokens, the compute-optimal token target, tokens the
# │          original run processed, passes over the corpus, and the days and
# │          energy one H100 machine needs for that budget.
# │ How:     Registry corpus size and training FLOPs, Chinchilla constants from
# │          the literature registry, H100 peak rate, TDP, and reference MFU.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Literature
from mlsysim.engine import calibration
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, byte, count, param, flop, second, day, kWh, joule
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_count, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_sci_flops, fmt_time, fmt_energy, fmt_ratio

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class GPT2DataWall:
    """GPT-2 XL on one eight-accelerator machine: compute outruns its own corpus."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    gpt2 = Models.Language.GPT2
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    corpus_bytes = gpt2.training_dataset_size  # WebText
    training_flops = gpt2.training_ops  # estimate for the original run
    flops_per_param_token = Literature.Chinchilla.ComputeConstant.value * flop / (param * count)
    tokens_per_param_opt = Literature.Chinchilla.TokensPerParam.value
    mfu = Literature.Training.MfuHigh  # same utilization as the training chapter's GPT-2 run
    bytes_per_token = 4 * byte / count  # scenario assumption: English text averages about 4 bytes per BPE token
    node_accelerators = 8  # one machine at the top of this book's scope

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params = gpt2.parameters.to(param).magnitude
    unique_tokens = (corpus_bytes / bytes_per_token).to(count)
    optimal_tokens = tokens_per_param_opt * params * count
    shortfall = (optimal_tokens / unique_tokens).to("").magnitude
    tokens_per_param_have = unique_tokens.magnitude / params
    tokens_processed = (training_flops / (flops_per_param_token * gpt2.parameters.to(param))).to(count)
    corpus_passes = (tokens_processed / unique_tokens).to("").magnitude
    node_rate = node_accelerators * h100.compute.peak_flops * mfu
    node_time = (training_flops / node_rate).to(second)
    node_energy = (node_accelerators * h100.tdp * node_time).to(joule)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(9.5 < unique_tokens.magnitude / 1e9 < 10.5, f"Prose says about 10 billion unique tokens, got {unique_tokens}.")
    check(2.9 < shortfall < 3.1, f"Prose says the fitted balance asks for 3x WebText, got {shortfall:.2f}.")
    check(16 < corpus_passes < 17.5, f"Prose says about 17 passes over WebText, got {corpus_passes:.1f}.")
    # Must agree with the training chapter's run (35 days, about 590 kWh on one H100)
    check(4.2 < node_time.to(day).magnitude < 4.6, f"Expected about 4.4 days on eight H100s, got {node_time.to(day)}.")
    check(550 < node_energy.to(kWh).magnitude < 620, f"Energy must match the one-H100 run, about 590 kWh, got {node_energy.to(kWh)}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    corpus_gb_str = fmt_memory(corpus_bytes, unit=GB, precision=0)
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_count(bytes_per_token.magnitude, precision=0, commas=False)
    params_str = fmt_count(gpt2.parameters.to(param).magnitude, scale='B', precision=1, scale_style='word')
    unique_tokens_str = fmt_count(unique_tokens, scale='B', precision=0, commas=False, scale_style='word')
    tokens_per_param_opt_str = fmt_count(tokens_per_param_opt, precision=0, commas=False)
    tokens_per_param_have_str = fmt_ratio(tokens_per_param_have, precision=1)
    optimal_tokens_str = fmt_count(optimal_tokens, scale='B', precision=0, commas=False, scale_style='word')
    shortfall_mult_str = fmt_multiple(shortfall, precision=0)
    training_flops_str = fmt_sci_flops(training_flops, precision=1)
    tokens_processed_str = fmt_count(round(tokens_processed.magnitude, -9), scale='B', precision=0, commas=False, scale_style='word')
    corpus_passes_str = fmt_count(round(corpus_passes), precision=0, commas=False)
    mfu_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(mfu, 2), precision=0, style='prose')
    node_accelerators_str = fmt_count(node_accelerators, precision=0, commas=False)
    node_days_str = fmt_time(node_time, 'day', precision=1, style='word')
    node_energy_kwh_str = fmt_energy(round(node_energy.to(kWh).magnitude, -1) * kWh, unit=kWh, precision=0, commas=True)
```

WebText, GPT-2's training corpus [@radford2019language], holds `{python} GPT2DataWall.corpus_gb_str` of text, about `{python} GPT2DataWall.unique_tokens_str` tokens at roughly `{python} GPT2DataWall.bytes_per_token_str` bytes per token. The compute-optimal balance fitted by the Chinchilla study, about `{python} GPT2DataWall.tokens_per_param_opt_str` training tokens per parameter (developed in @sec-data-selection-computeoptimal-frontier-24ba), asks for `{python} GPT2DataWall.optimal_tokens_str` unique tokens for GPT-2's `{python} GPT2DataWall.params_str` parameters, `{python} GPT2DataWall.shortfall_mult_str` what WebText holds. The original run spent about `{python} GPT2DataWall.training_flops_str`, which at six FLOPs per parameter per token processed about `{python} GPT2DataWall.tokens_processed_str` tokens, so the model saw its corpus roughly `{python} GPT2DataWall.corpus_passes_str` times. One machine with `{python} GPT2DataWall.node_accelerators_str` H100 accelerators running at `{python} GPT2DataWall.mfu_pct_str` model FLOPs utilization (MFU), the fraction of peak arithmetic a training run actually delivers (definition \ref{dfn-training-model-flops-utilization-mfu}), completes that budget in about `{python} GPT2DataWall.node_days_str` and `{python} GPT2DataWall.node_energy_kwh_str` of accelerator energy. Less than a week of one machine's compute therefore passes over the whole corpus many times. An engineering team in that position can repeat epochs over the same text, but gradient updates on familiar tokens yield diminishing loss reductions. It can lower quality thresholds to admit uncurated web text, but noisy and misaligned tokens degrade downstream evaluation. Its third option is to invest in data selection (refining quality filters, constructing difficulty curricula, and synthesizing missing edge cases) to raise the learning return per FLOP.

When *compute* is abundant and *quality data* is scarce, the optimization priority inverts. Selection, not faster kernels, then extracts more learning per dollar, and for teams whose accelerator budget exceeds their curated corpus, the bottleneck shifts from accelerator access to the quality, legality, and diversity of the training data.

The bitter lesson applies here in data terms. A filter written from human intuition about which examples matter is the hand-built expertise the lesson warns against, whereas selection that uses the model's own signals, such as loss, gradient norms, or embedding similarity, scales with compute. Either way, improved rankings must be established against downstream quality and coverage.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The bitter lesson, that general methods using more computation outperform encoded human expertise, is established in @sec-introduction-bitter-lesson-79c7.
:::

Data engineering makes data correct; data selection asks which correct examples are worth training on. When selection removes processing at matched quality, it shrinks the total operations $(\Operations)$ term in the iron law\index{Iron law of ML systems!total operations reduction via data selection} (principle \ref{pri-iron-law}). It therefore starts by making sample value explicit relative to compute cost. The information-compute ratio measures that value as learning signal gained per unit of training compute, formalized in @sec-data-selection-informationcompute-ratio-8c0b.

::: {#dfn-data-selection-data-selection .callout-definition title="Data selection"}

***Data selection***\index{Data selection!definition} is the process of retaining, prioritizing, or generating training examples to minimize the end-to-end cost of reaching target quality while preserving required coverage.

1.  **Significance**: Each excluded example removes a forward pass, a backward pass, and an optimizer update, so selection reduces the total operations $(\Operations)$ directly.
2.  **Distinction**: A dataset can pass every data engineering check and still contain many examples that teach the model nothing new; selection judges informativeness and diversity, not correctness.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Minimizing dataset size instead of end-to-end cost. Scoring, labeling, and lost coverage can erase the savings of a smaller set.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: data-selection-savings-calc

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ IRON LAW SAVINGS CALCULATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Data Selection and the Iron Law" callout
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the multiplicative impact of data selection.
# │ Show: That dataset reduction compounds with hardware and model optimizations.
# │ How: Contrast additive vs. multiplicative speedup factors for an 8x total gain.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt, fmt_usd, check
from mlsysim import Infrastructure
from mlsysim.core.units import MILLION, USD, hour

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class IronLawSavings:
    """
    Namespace for Iron Law Multiplicative Savings.
    Scenario: 2x Data Selection * 2x Compression * 2x Hardware = 8x Total.
    """

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Optimization factors
    factor_data = 2.0
    factor_model = 2.0
    factor_hw = 2.0

    # Derived
    data_pruning_pct = (1 - (1 / factor_data)) * 100

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Step 1: Multiplicative effect
    total_speedup = factor_data * factor_model * factor_hw

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    additive_sum = factor_data + factor_model + factor_hw
    check(total_speedup > additive_sum, f"Multiplicative speedup ({total_speedup}x) should exceed additive sum ({additive_sum}).")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    dataset_reduction_pct_str = fmt_percent(data_pruning_pct / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    combined_factor_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(total_speedup), precision=0, commas=False)
    factor_data_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(factor_data), precision=0, commas=False)
    factor_model_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(factor_model), precision=0, commas=False)
    factor_hw_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(factor_hw), precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {#psp-data-selection-data-selection-iron-law .callout-perspective title="Data selection and the iron law"}

In the iron law of ML systems $(\Time= \frac{\DataVolume}{\Bandwidth} + \frac{\Operations}{\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw} + \Latency)$, data selection reduces the number of examples or tokens that enter the workload. Later model-level optimizations reduce operations per forward/backward pass, and machine-level optimizations increase $\PeakRate$ (peak throughput) and $\EfficiencyHw$ (utilization). Selection removes work before those downstream optimizations execute it.

Within the compute term $\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$, data selection is multiplicatively valuable\index{Iron law of ML systems!multiplicative savings from data selection}. Data selection and model-level optimization shrink the numerator while machine-level optimization enlarges the denominator, so when a compute-bound run applies all three, a `{python} IronLawSavings.factor_data_mult_str` reduction in dataset size with `{python} IronLawSavings.factor_model_mult_str` fewer operations per sample and `{python} IronLawSavings.factor_hw_mult_str` higher effective throughput yields an `{python} IronLawSavings.combined_factor_mult_str` reduction in compute time because the factors multiply; each layer divides the work the next layer sees. The iron law itself remains the sum of @eq-intro-iron-law, so a run bound by data movement $(\DataVolume/\Bandwidth)$ or fixed overhead $(\Latency)$ sees less than the full product.

:::

Holding epoch count, batch size, and per-sample work fixed, a `{python} IronLawSavings.dataset_reduction_pct_str` reduction in dataset size directly halves the required forward passes, backward passes, and gradient updates. For the GPT-2 run above, it would halve both the `{python} GPT2DataWall.node_days_str` on one eight-H100 machine and the `{python} GPT2DataWall.node_energy_kwh_str` of accelerator energy, provided the training schedule does not compensate by adding optimization steps.

These compute savings propagate throughout the hardware hierarchy. By decreasing total data volume ($\DataVolume$), deduplication\index{Deduplication!storage and I/O cost reduction} and coreset selection alleviate storage bandwidth demands, network fabric ingress, and host-to-accelerator PCIe transfers that otherwise leave the accelerator's arithmetic units waiting on input. Upstream, active learning\index{Active learning!labeling cost reduction} curbs annotation budgets by directing human labeling to samples chosen for uncertainty, diversity, or other task-relevant query criteria.

Yet selection is not free. Every selection strategy incurs its own runtime overhead to score, filter, shuffle, or coordinate samples. An online selection algorithm that executes additional forward passes to rank sample difficulty can easily consume more accelerator cycles than it saves if its selection overhead exceeds the subsequent reduction in training time. A pipeline claiming a training-time saving must make filtering plus subset training faster than full-data training at the same target quality, the selection inequality of @sec-data-selection-selection-inequality-3b7e. Labeling savings and reusable representations require the broader cost accounting of @sec-data-selection-decision-framework-0261.

A learning-theory view of this problem counts the samples needed to reach a test error and treats each sample as free. The systems view counts the FLOPs, bytes, labels, seconds, and joules needed to reach the same quality, including the cost of choosing the samples. In the D·A·M taxonomy\index{DAM taxonomy@D·A·M taxonomy!data selection}, data selection works on the data axis, deciding whether an example warrants processing at all before the algorithm fixes the operations each example costs and the machine fixes how fast those operations run. Removing an example therefore lightens both adjacent boundaries, the storage and input traffic between data and machine and the learning return between data and algorithm.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The D·A·M taxonomy and its three diagnostic axes are established in @sec-introduction-defining-ml-systems-d4af.
:::

The engineering toolkit for intelligent data selection follows a deliberate optimization ordering\index{Data selection!optimization ordering}, first asking whether a sample is worth processing and only then how to process the remaining workload efficiently. Static pruning\index{Static pruning!definition} fixes the retained subset before target-model training; scoring may itself require proxy training. Dynamic selection\index{Dynamic selection!definition} adapts which examples the training loop sees, and which receive labels, as training proceeds, through curriculum learning and active learning. Synthetic generation\index{Synthetic data generation!definition} creates high-value samples through augmentation, simulation, or examples labeled by a larger trained model (a *teacher*) when real data runs short.

Learning from unlabeled data complements these three levers by redefining what constitutes a supervision signal; rather than selecting among labeled examples, semi-supervised and self-supervised methods derive learning targets from the structure of unannotated data. Which levers to use, and in what order, depends on the workload (@fig-data-selection-pipeline).

::: {#fig-data-selection-pipeline fig-cap="**An Example Data Selection Pipeline**: One possible combination of interventions for increasing data value. The three intervention points are Static Pruning before target training, Dynamic Selection during training, and Synthetic Generation on demand. The sequence is illustrative rather than required: synthetic data can enter independently and can itself be pruned or dynamically selected. The final evaluation determines whether the quality gain justifies the compute cost through the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR)." fig-alt="Illustrative flow diagram from raw data through static pruning, dynamic selection, and synthetic generation to a model. The final arrow is labeled Evaluate ICR. Labels place pruning before target training, dynamic selection during training, and generation on demand."}

:::

Two lighthouses carry the chapter, each in its own role. GPT-2 XL, bandwidth-bound when it decodes one token at a time but compute-bound when it trains on long batches (@sec-model-training), carries the wall itself, the compute-optimal diagnosis of whether a run is data-starved, and token-level deduplication. ResNet-50 on ImageNet\index{ResNet-50!data selection}, the book's compute-bound lighthouse, carries coresets, labels, augmentation, the input pipeline that must feed it, and the decision of which lever to fund. Its training crosses into an input-bound regime whenever the host cannot decode images as fast as the accelerator consumes them (@sec-model-training-staged-pipeline), and that crossing returns when selection runs on the machine. The measures of value in the next section use both. Both lighthouses run on the book's reference machine, the H100, so every saving can be stated in accelerator seconds and joules. The recommendation lighthouse (DLRM), MobileNetV2, and keyword spotting return only in the closing comparison of @sec-data-selection-decision-framework-0261, where each turns out to be bound by a different resource.

Every lever in the chapter removes work at one stage of the machine and adds work of its own, so each must pass a test before it is accepted (@tbl-data-selection-chapter-spine). Measuring data value builds the yardsticks: the information-compute ratio, learning-curve metrics, the compute-optimal diagnosis, and the selection inequality. Static pruning removes duplicates, defective records, and redundant examples before training. Dynamic selection reorders examples and chooses which ones receive labels as the model learns. Synthetic data generation creates the examples the corpus lacks, and learning from unlabeled data replaces labels with structure the data already contains. Selection engineering runs those levers on the machine without starving the accelerator, including across several accelerators. Choosing a selection strategy compares the cost of each lever and picks among them, and the cross-layer section hands the curated result to model compression.

| **Section**                       | **Lever and when it acts**                                  | **Work it removes**                          | **Work it adds**                                             | **Test it must pass**                                         |
|:----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Measuring Data Value**          | Yardsticks for every lever                                  | None                                         | Pilot runs at several data sizes                             | Defines the tests below                                       |
| **Static Pruning**                | Deduplication, quality filtering, coreset; before training  | Tokens and examples processed in every epoch | Hashing and proxy scoring passes                             | Selection inequality at matched quality and coverage          |
| **Dynamic Selection**             | Curriculum learning, active learning; during training       | Warmup FLOPs; labels                         | Difficulty scoring, pool scoring rounds, retraining          | Time to target quality; label cost against a random baseline  |
| **Synthetic Data Generation**     | Augmentation, generative synthesis, distillation; on demand | Collection and labeling of scarce cases      | Host transforms, generator inference, stored teacher targets | Validation on real deployment data                            |
| **Learning from Unlabeled Data**  | Semi-supervised and self-supervised learning                | Task-specific labels                         | Extra training compute; pretraining                          | Total label and compute cost; reuse across tasks              |
| **Selection Engineering**         | Running any lever on the machine                            | Accelerator idle time                        | Scoring latency, random reads, worker coordination           | The accelerator stays fed and the inequality holds end to end |
| **Choosing a Selection Strategy** | Costing the levers and picking among them                   | Investment in levers that do not pay         | Engineering and infrastructure investment                    | Return on investment over the runs that share it              |

: **Chapter Map**: Each section of the chapter, the work its lever removes and adds on the machine, and the test the lever must pass before it is accepted. {#tbl-data-selection-chapter-spine tbl-colwidths="[18,22,20,20,20]"}

Each test in the right-hand column depends on measuring what an example is worth, the subject of the next section.

## Measuring Data Value {#sec-data-selection-measurement-framework-733b}

A ResNet-50 trained on an aggressively filtered ImageNet subset can hold its aggregate accuracy while failing on rare classes that the filter discarded as low-density noise, and a GPT-2 run on a filtered corpus can cost less per epoch while needing more epochs to reach the same loss. A measurement framework\index{Measurement framework!data selection metrics} is therefore needed to show what a reduction actually saves. Every data selection technique claims to improve efficiency, but only measurement separates genuine training savings from work that has merely moved to another pipeline stage, or from degradation on safety-critical tail distributions. The measures build from the information-compute ratio through metrics that tie sample reduction to accuracy and a diagnostic of whether a run is data-limited, to the selection inequality that every training-time claim must satisfy.

### The information-compute ratio {#sec-data-selection-informationcompute-ratio-8c0b}

The data wall calls for a quantitative measure of what each example returns. Data selection moves along a Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) between accuracy and cost\index{Information-compute ratio!accuracy-cost frontier}, the set of operating points that no alternative beats on one objective without losing on the other. Retaining every example preserves coverage but expends compute on redundant signal, whereas over-aggressive pruning saves FLOPs at the expense of rare-slice recall. Navigating that trade-off requires quantifying the marginal learning signal each sample yields per unit of hardware execution. Data engineering already measured task-relevant signal against one cost, the data gravity of moving bytes, in the data selection gain of @eq-data-selection-gain. Selection needs the same ratio with training compute in the denominator, because a sample that is cheap to move can still cost a full forward and backward pass. That ratio is the **information-compute ratio** (ICR)\index{Information-compute ratio!definition}.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Locating a model's operating point on the accuracy-efficiency frontier, and moving along it with compression, is developed in @sec-model-compression-balancing-tradeoffs-6ae3.
:::

Let $\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent$ be the learning signal a sample or batch adds and $\FiniteChange\Operations$ the training operations spent processing it. In practice $\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent$ is measured as the gain in a fixed evaluation metric, such as percentage points of validation accuracy, so ICR carries units of metric gain per FLOP. The ratio relates the two:
$$\text{ICR} = \frac{\FiniteChange\DataInformationContent}{\FiniteChange\Operations}$$

A higher ICR indicates that each FLOP of training yields more measured learning signal over the stated interval. Validation gain and training FLOPs can be observed for a specified experiment with a fixed evaluation protocol; the causal contribution of an individual example generally cannot. Uncertainty and gradient-based scores instead rank candidate examples before their downstream benefit is known. Those rankings require validation against measured quality, compute cost, and deployment-critical slice coverage. The core metrics in @sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9 supply complementary evidence for that evaluation rather than interchangeable measurements of per-example information.

### Diminishing returns and the ICR frontier {#sec-data-selection-icr-frontier}

The information-compute ratio falls as increasingly redundant examples enter the dataset. The **ICR frontier**\index{Information-compute ratio!frontier} is the dataset size beyond which the marginal ICR, the learning returned by the next FLOP spent on more data, drops below what that FLOP could return elsewhere: a larger model, a different data source, or an earlier stop.

To illustrate diminishing returns, let $\DataInformationContent(\DatasetSize)$ be the information content of a dataset of size $\DatasetSize$ and assume $\DataInformationContent(\DatasetSize) \propto \log \DatasetSize$. This is a simplified analytical model rather than a universal law. If compute cost scales linearly with the per-sample operation count $\OperationsPerSample$, then total operations are $\Operations = \OperationsPerSample \cdot \DatasetSize$, and the resulting marginal ICR follows @eq-icr-decay:
$$\text{ICR}(\DatasetSize) = \frac{\DerivativeOperator\DataInformationContent/d\DatasetSize}{d\Operations/d\DatasetSize} \approx \frac{1/\DatasetSize}{\OperationsPerSample} = \frac{1}{\OperationsPerSample\cdot \DatasetSize}$$ {#eq-icr-decay}

The derivative ratio describes the return on an infinitesimal increase in dataset size. For two controlled finite allocations, the corresponding incremental ratio divides the additional evaluation gain by the additional training FLOPs, using the same evaluation metric and protocol. The coreset comparison that follows instead averages gain over one epoch of each dataset; that average does not establish the return on the next increment.

Under this illustrative model, marginal ICR falls as $1/(\OperationsPerSample \cdot \DatasetSize)$, so doubling the dataset halves the learning each additional FLOP yields. Inverted, the compute spent per unit of learning grows linearly with $\DatasetSize$. ICR never reaches zero in this model and the curve has no knee of its own, so the frontier is located by comparing marginal ICR with the threshold the engineer sets, not read off the curve. That saturation is distinct from the data wall (a limit on how much new, high-quality data exists), but the two compound\index{Data wall!zero learning signal}. When new data is scarce *and* marginal data is weak, selection becomes the main lever. Beyond the frontier, additional data still adds compute but returns less learning than the threshold demands. In this regime additional data inflates the $\Operations$ term of the iron law\index{Information-compute ratio!diminishing returns} without a commensurate gain in ICR. Measured in dollars rather than FLOPs, the same excess lowers the return on compute (RoC) of @eq-intro-roc, the accuracy gained per added dollar of infrastructure.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Return on compute, the economic lens that measures accuracy gains against infrastructure spending, is established in @sec-introduction-roc-invariant.
:::

Data selection turns the total operations $(\Operations)$ term in the iron law from a fixed constant into a variable. A 2$\times$ improvement in measured ICR halves the FLOPs required to reach the same measured gain. It produces the same ideal time reduction as a 2$\times$ throughput increase only when the workload is compute-bound and the saved work lies on the critical path. ICR focuses specifically on compute; the cost model of @sec-data-selection-quantifying-data-costs-roi-f0b4 extends the same reasoning to acquisition, labeling, and storage costs.

The ratio becomes concrete on a *coreset*\index{Coreset!ICR example}, a deliberately selected subset intended to preserve the full dataset's learning signal. Computing ICR for an ImageNet coreset used to train the ResNet-50 lighthouse shows how large the efficiency gap could become once dataset size, per-sample model cost, and selection strategy meet concrete FLOP budgets. The scenario uses assumed accuracy gains to illustrate the arithmetic; it is not a reported result for the scoring method (EL2N) that @sec-data-selection-coreset-selection-algorithms-2c74 develops.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: data-selection-setup

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ICR CORESET COMPARISON
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Computing ICR: Coresets" callout example
# │
# │ Goal: Make the Information-Compute Ratio (ICR) concrete.
# │ Show: That coresets achieve 1.8× higher ICR by focusing on difficult samples.
# │ How: Compare learning-per-FLOP for random sampling vs. coreset selection.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Datasets, Models
from mlsysim.core.units import GFLOPs, count, flop
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt, fmt_math, check, fmt_flops, fmt_pp, fmt_sci_flops, fmt_count, sci_latex

class IcrCoresetComparison:
    """Illustrative learning-per-FLOP comparison for random and selected data."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    imagenet_size = Datasets.ImageNet.training_examples.to(count)
    acc_gain_random_pp = 5.0  # percentage-point gain per epoch
    acc_gain_coreset_pp = 4.5  # percentage points with 50% coreset
    coreset_fraction_value = 0.5  # keep 50% of data

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    m_resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    resnet50_fwd_flops = m_resnet.inference_flops.to(GFLOPs)
    resnet50_fwdbwd_flops = (m_resnet.inference_flops * 3).to(GFLOPs)
    full_epoch_flops = imagenet_size * resnet50_fwdbwd_flops

    icr_random_value = acc_gain_random_pp / full_epoch_flops.to(flop).magnitude

    coreset_size = imagenet_size * coreset_fraction_value
    coreset_flops = coreset_size * resnet50_fwdbwd_flops
    icr_coreset_value = acc_gain_coreset_pp / coreset_flops.to(flop).magnitude
    icr_ratio_value = icr_coreset_value / icr_random_value
    acc_diff_pp = acc_gain_random_pp - acc_gain_coreset_pp

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(icr_ratio_value > 1.0, f"Coreset ICR ({icr_ratio_value:.2f}) should exceed random ICR.")
    check(coreset_fraction_value < 1.0, "Coreset fraction must be less than 1.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    resnet50_fwd_gflop_str = fmt_flops(resnet50_fwd_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1)
    resnet50_fwdbwd_gflop_str = fmt_flops(resnet50_fwdbwd_flops, unit=GFLOPs, precision=1)
    full_epoch_flops_str = fmt_sci_flops(full_epoch_flops, precision=1)
    icr_random_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(icr_random_value, precision=1))
    imagenet_size_str = fmt_count(imagenet_size, scale='M', precision=2)
    # Custom "K" suffix on a divided count uses fmt() suffix discipline.
    coreset_size_str = fmt_count(coreset_size, scale='K', precision=1, commas=False)
    coreset_flops_str = fmt_sci_flops(coreset_flops, precision=1)
    icr_coreset_math = fmt_math(sci_latex(icr_coreset_value, precision=1))
    icr_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(icr_ratio_value, precision=1, commas=False)
    acc_gain_random_str = fmt_pp(acc_gain_random_pp, precision=0)
    acc_gain_coreset_str = fmt_pp(acc_gain_coreset_pp, precision=1)
    acc_diff_str = fmt_pp(acc_diff_pp, precision=1)
    coreset_pct_str = fmt_percent(coreset_fraction_value, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    acc_perf_pct_str = fmt_percent(acc_gain_coreset_pp / acc_gain_random_pp, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {#nbk-data-selection-computing-icr-coresets .callout-notebook title="Computing ICR: Coresets"}

**Problem**: Training the ResNet-50 lighthouse model on ImageNet for one epoch costs `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.full_epoch_flops_str`. Under the scenario's assumed accuracy gains, how would retaining `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.coreset_pct_str` of the data change the information-compute ratio? The calculation holds the per-sample work fixed and does not include selection overhead.

**Setup**:

- Dataset: ImageNet (`{python} IcrCoresetComparison.imagenet_size_str`)
- Model: ResNet-50 lighthouse (~`{python} IcrCoresetComparison.resnet50_fwd_gflop_str` per forward pass, roughly `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.resnet50_fwdbwd_gflop_str` for a forward plus backward training step, depending on implementation)
- One epoch: `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.imagenet_size_str` $\times$ `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.resnet50_fwdbwd_gflop_str` = `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.full_epoch_flops_str`
- Assumed accuracy improvement per epoch (early training): `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_random_str`

**Random selection (baseline)**:

- Process all `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.imagenet_size_str` samples uniformly
- Accuracy gain: `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_random_str`
- $\text{ICR}_{\text{random}}$ = `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_random_str` / (`{python} IcrCoresetComparison.full_epoch_flops_str`) = `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.icr_random_math` per FLOP

**Difficulty-scored coreset** (EL2N, a training-dynamics score defined in @sec-data-selection-coreset-selection-algorithms-2c74; `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.coreset_pct_str` of data):

- Process `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.coreset_size_str` selected samples
- Assumed accuracy gain: `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_coreset_str` (`{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_perf_pct_str` of the full-data gain)
- Compute: `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.coreset_size_str` $\times$ `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.resnet50_fwdbwd_gflop_str` = `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.coreset_flops_str`
- $\text{ICR}_{\text{coreset}}$ = `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_coreset_str` / (`{python} IcrCoresetComparison.coreset_flops_str`) = `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.icr_coreset_math` per FLOP

**Systems insight**: Under these assumptions, the selected subset achieves `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.icr_ratio_mult_str` higher ICR with a `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_diff_str` smaller accuracy gain. The comparison is learning per FLOP over one epoch of each dataset. It does not show that the coreset reaches the full-data run's final accuracy, which must be checked separately at equal quality, and a real decision also requires measured gains, selection overhead, and coverage checks.

:::

::: {#chk-data-selection-data-selection-efficiency .callout-checkpoint title="Data selection efficiency"}

The goal is to improve ICR subject to target quality and required coverage, then verify that the resulting pipeline reduces the cost it is intended to address.

**Metric checks**

- [ ] **ICR application**: Given two training runs with identical accuracy gains but different compute budgets, determine which achieved higher ICR.
- [ ] **Data efficiency**: The coreset notebook reports `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.icr_ratio_mult_str` higher ICR but a smaller per-epoch gain. Explain what would have to change for a 50 percent subset to match the full-data gain, which would give it 2$\times$ higher ICR and so deliver the same measured gain for half the training FLOPs.

**Pipeline checks**

- [ ] **The three stages**: Map static pruning, dynamic selection, and synthetic generation to the training lifecycle.

:::

A reduction in sample count remains a claim until it is shown to translate into end-to-end efficiency without silently compromising generalization. Notebook \ref{nbk-data-selection-computing-icr-coresets} holds per-sample work fixed and assumes its accuracy gains; testing the claim on a real workload requires measured metrics that weigh arithmetic savings, data movement overhead, and task quality across the complete pipeline.

### Core metrics {#sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9}

Three core metrics connect sample reduction to model quality instead of reporting accuracy alone. Performance-per-data measures accuracy gain per sample, the area under the learning curve measures cumulative learning efficiency across dataset scales, and the data compression ratio measures dataset reduction at a target accuracy. Together they complement the measured information-compute ratio (@sec-data-selection-informationcompute-ratio-8c0b). PPD measures average gain per sample, which becomes gain per FLOP once per-sample cost is fixed. AULC summarizes performance across a common dataset-size range, while DCR measures retained sample reduction at fixed quality. None establishes the causal value of an individual example.

#### Performance-per-data {.unnumbered}

The most direct metric, **performance-per-data (PPD)**\index{Performance-per-data!metric definition}, measures accuracy gain per sample:
$$
\text{PPD}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) = \frac{\text{Accuracy}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) - \text{Accuracy}(0)}{\LearningCurveSampleCount}
$$
where $\LearningCurveSampleCount$ is the number of training samples. A higher PPD indicates greater average improvement per sample over the stated interval. Its shape must be measured because diminishing returns and their onset are workload-dependent.

#### Area under the learning curve {.unnumbered}

Rather than comparing at a single point, the **area under the learning curve**\index{Area under the learning curve!definition} (AULC) integrates performance across all dataset sizes:
$$
\text{AULC} = \int_0^\DatasetSize\text{Accuracy}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) \, d\LearningCurveSampleCount$$
where $\LearningCurveSampleCount$ is the dataset size and $\DatasetSize$ is the total dataset size.

For the same metric and integration range, a higher AULC means stronger integrated performance across dataset sizes, though one strategy need not outperform the other at every size. Comparisons must use the same upper limit $\DatasetSize$ or normalize the integral. Measuring AULC requires training at several dataset sizes, so the metric itself spends compute, and when it guides a selection decision that cost belongs to the selection overhead.

#### Data compression ratio {.unnumbered}

For coreset methods, the **data compression ratio**\index{Data compression ratio!definition} (DCR) measures how much data reduction is achieved at a target accuracy:
$$
\text{DCR} = \frac{\FullDatasetSize}{\SubsetDatasetSize} \text{ at } \text{Accuracy}_{\text{target}}
$$

A DCR of 5$\times$ means the coreset achieves target accuracy with 20 percent of the data.

Applied to the coreset notebook, the three metrics behave differently. Over one epoch, the full ImageNet set gains `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_random_str` while the half-size coreset gains `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.acc_gain_coreset_str`, so the coreset's PPD is higher by the same `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.icr_ratio_mult_str` as its ICR, because per-sample work is fixed. DCR cannot be computed from that notebook at all, because the two runs never reach a common target accuracy. Exposing that missing equal-quality check is exactly the job DCR is designed for.

### The compute-optimal frontier {#sec-data-selection-computeoptimal-frontier-24ba}

While the core metrics in @sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9 measure individual techniques, a higher-level diagnostic is also needed to test whether the overall training strategy is data-limited or compute-limited. Neural scaling-law experiments [@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022chinchilla] fit power-law relationships over particular model families, datasets, and compute ranges. Controlled sweeps can use those fitted relationships to compare model and data allocations, but no single ratio diagnoses every training run.

The Chinchilla study\index{Chinchilla!compute-optimal training}[^fn-chinchilla-scaling-law] [@hoffmann2022chinchilla] fit a compute-optimal balance between model size and training data within its experimental regime. Allocations on either side of that fitted balance used the study's compute budget less effectively.

[^fn-chinchilla-scaling-law]: **Chinchilla**\index{Chinchilla!compute-optimal scaling}: Chinchilla is a 70-billion-parameter language model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens. In the experiments reported by @hoffmann2022chinchilla, it outperformed the larger GPT-3 on most evaluated tasks under a similar training-compute budget. The fitted compute-optimal allocation scaled parameters and tokens at roughly equal rates within the study's experimental regime; it is not a universal prescription for every architecture, dataset, or training recipe.

The optimal balance defines a **compute-optimal frontier**\index{Compute-optimal frontier!Chinchilla scaling laws}: the best achievable performance at each compute budget when data and model size are properly balanced. Plotted over normalized training compute, the frontier separates the optimal operating envelope from the compute-starved and data-starved allocations in the suboptimal region below it (@fig-compute-optimal-frontier).

::: {#fig-compute-optimal-frontier fig-env="figure" fig-pos="H" fig-cap="**Illustrative Compute-Optimal Frontier**: The green curve is a conceptual frontier over normalized compute, not a fitted result from Chinchilla. Points below it illustrate allocations that a controlled model-size and token-count sweep might identify as data- or compute-limited." fig-alt="Semi-log plot with normalized training compute from 10^0 to 10^3 on the logarithmic x-axis and model performance from 50 to 100 on the y-axis. A green compute-optimal frontier bounds a gray-shaded suboptimal region. Orange Data-starved and red Compute-starved points below the curve have dashed arrows labeled Better data selection and More training, respectively; a violet Optimal point lies on the curve."}

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMPUTE-OPTIMAL FRONTIER (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-compute-optimal-frontier—Measuring Data Selection section

# │ Show: Log-log axes; green frontier curve; orange/red/purple points; labels.

# │

# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 3.6))

# Compute-optimal frontier curve

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

# Suboptimal region fill

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.fill_between(x, 50, y, color='gray', alpha=0.08)

# Frontier curve
ax.plot(x, y, color=COLORS['GreenLine'], linewidth=2.5, label='Compute-optimal frontier', zorder=3)

# Data-starved point
ax.scatter([100], [72], color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], s=100, zorder=4, edgecolors='white')

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.annotate('', xy=(100, 83), xytext=(100, 73), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=COLORS['OrangeLine'], lw=1.5, linestyle='dashed'))
ax.text(
    110,
    78,
    'Better data\nselection',
    fontsize=9,
    color=COLORS['OrangeLine'],
    va='center',

ax.annotate('', xy=(28, 74), xytext=(11, 63), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=1.5, linestyle='dashed'))
ax.text(
    12,
    68,

    60,

    fontsize=9,
    fontweight='bold',

    ha='center',
    va='center',
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', edgecolor='none', alpha=0.9, pad=2),

# Optimal point—lands exactly on the frontier curve y = 95 - 45 * x^-0.8 at x = 300.

ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_xlabel('Training Compute (normalized units)')
ax.set_ylabel('Model Performance (Accuracy)')

ax.set_ylim(50, 100)
ax.set_xticks([1, 10, 100, 1000])
ax.set_xticklabels(['$10^0$', '$10^1$', '$10^2$', '$10^3$'])

```

:::

The frontier answers one allocation question, whether the next unit of compute at a given budget should go to more parameters or to more training tokens. A run is *data-starved* when it trains on too few unique, useful tokens for its parameter count, so its tokens-per-parameter ratio sits well under the fitted balance, and the same compute would yield more accuracy with more or better data. Against a frontier fitted from controlled sweeps, an operating point's location motivates further experiments. The directional vectors charted in @fig-compute-optimal-frontier illustrate two candidate interventions: additional training compute and improved data selection at fixed compute. Controlled changes to model size, data, and training allocation determine which intervention helps; a point below the frontier does not identify a unique remedy. Points near a fitted frontier remain specific to the model family, dataset, objective, and compute range used to estimate it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: chinchilla-diagnostic-calc

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHINCHILLA D/P DIAGNOSTIC ANCHORS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Interpreting the Chinchilla result" subsection and the
# │          [^fn-chinchilla-token-ratio] footnote.
# │
# │ Goal:    Anchor the GPT-3 / Llama 2 70B reference D/P ratios.
# │ Show:    Reference D/P ratios for both models and the
# │          token-count growth implied by doubling the compute budget.
# │ How:     Divide training tokens by parameter counts for each reference
# │          model; compute sqrt(2) - 1 for the doubling growth percent.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math

import mlsysim.core.units as c
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt_ratio

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class ChinchillaDiagnostic:
    # LOAD
    from mlsysim import Models

    m_gpt3 = Models.Language.GPT3
    m_llama2 = Models.Language.Llama2_70B

    tokens_per_param_opt = 20
    llama2_70b_training_tokens = 2.0 * c.TRILLION * c.count
    compute_multiplier = 2.0

    # EXECUTE
    gpt3_dn_ratio = (Models.Language.GPT3.training_tokens.to(c.count) / m_gpt3.parameters.to(c.param)).to("").magnitude
    llama2_dn_ratio = (llama2_70b_training_tokens / m_llama2.parameters.to(c.param)).to("").magnitude
    doubling_token_growth_pct = (math.sqrt(compute_multiplier) - 1) * 100

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tokens_per_param_opt_str = fmt_ratio(tokens_per_param_opt, precision=0, commas=False)
    gpt3_dn_ratio_str = fmt_ratio(gpt3_dn_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
    llama2_dn_ratio_str = fmt_ratio(llama2_dn_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
    doubling_token_growth_pct_str = fmt_percent(doubling_token_growth_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

#### Interpreting the Chinchilla result {.unnumbered}

Within the fitted Chinchilla regime, compute-optimal model parameters and training tokens grew at roughly equal rates.[^fn-chinchilla-token-ratio] Training a dense transformer costs approximately $6\Parameters\DatasetSize$ FLOPs for $\Parameters$ parameters and $\DatasetSize$ tokens, the forward-plus-backward accounting derived for the GPT-2 lighthouse in @sec-model-training-running-example-training-gpt2-19cd. Under an equal scaling regime where parameters and tokens grow proportionally ($\Parameters \propto \DatasetSize$), total compute scales quadratically ($\Operations \propto \DatasetSize^2$), directly implying that optimal token count scales as the square root of the compute budget ($\ComputeOptimalTokenCount \propto \sqrt{\Operations}$). Doubling compute therefore corresponds to about $\sqrt{2} - 1$, or `{python} ChinchillaDiagnostic.doubling_token_growth_pct_str`, more tokens under those assumptions. The commonly quoted `{python} ChinchillaDiagnostic.tokens_per_param_opt_str` tokens per parameter is a useful reference point from that study, not a universal optimum.

GPT-2 sits well short of that reference. WebText supplies about `{python} GPT2DataWall.tokens_per_param_have_str` unique tokens per parameter, a third of the fitted balance, and the original run made up the difference by repeating those tokens about `{python} GPT2DataWall.corpus_passes_str` times (@sec-data-selection-data-selection-fundamentals-e839). Repetition keeps the arithmetic budget but not the learning per FLOP, which is the regime where selection, rather than more compute, moves the run toward the frontier.

[^fn-chinchilla-token-ratio]: [offset=-1mm] **Tokens per parameter**\index{Chinchilla!tokens-per-parameter diagnostic}: The ratio $\DatasetSize/\Parameters$ compares training tokens with model parameters; GPT-3 used approximately `{python} ChinchillaDiagnostic.gpt3_dn_ratio_str` tokens per parameter [@brown2020language], while Llama 2 70B used approximately `{python} ChinchillaDiagnostic.llama2_dn_ratio_str` [@touvron2023llama2]. These descriptive ratios do not establish whether either run is compute-optimal under a different architecture, corpus, objective, or hardware budget. Controlled model-size and token-count sweeps are required for that diagnosis.

#### Applying the diagnostic {.unnumbered}

If a training run underperforms expectations, extending one run can reveal whether additional optimization steps still help, but a plateau does not identify data starvation by itself. Learning-rate schedules, optimization limits, model capacity, and data quality can all produce a plateau. A reliable diagnosis compares controlled runs that vary model size, token count, and compute allocation while holding the evaluation protocol fixed.

When controlled runs do point to the data, the remedy that keeps compute fixed is better selection, which changes the shape of the learning curve itself. Seeing that change requires switching axes, from the frontier's training compute to the core metrics' dataset size, where the area under each curve is the AULC defined in @sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9. In the illustrative curves of @fig-ppd-curve, efficient selection bends into an accuracy plateau near 25 percent of the data while uniform random sampling climbs gradually across the entire budget. The horizontal separation between the curves is the reduction in required samples, and at an identical 20 percent data budget the vertical gap is the accuracy that selection adds without any additional compute.

::: {#fig-ppd-curve fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Illustrative Diminishing Returns of Data**: The synthetic data-efficient curve (blue) reaches the same plateau with fewer samples than random sampling (gray). The vertical red arrow marks the modeled performance gap at a fixed dataset size; measured curves need not have this shape." fig-alt="Line chart with Dataset Size (% of Total) on the x-axis and Model Accuracy (%) on the y-axis. A gray dashed Random Sampling curve rises gradually, while a blue Efficient Selection curve rises more steeply and reaches the same plateau earlier; the area between them is lightly shaded blue. A vertical red double-headed arrow is labeled Performance Gap (Same Data Budget)."}

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DIMINISHING RETURNS FIGURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-ppd-curve (Measuring Data Selection section)
# │
# │ Goal: Visualize the performance benefits of data selection.
# │ Show: That efficient selection reaches the accuracy plateau faster than random sampling.
# │ How: Plot exponential saturation curves for random vs. curated datasets.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Visualize the performance benefits of data selection.
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 4))

# —Plot: Efficient vs Random Data Selection ---

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
x = np.linspace(0, 100, 200)
y_random = 95 * (1 - np.exp(-0.04 * x))
y_efficient = 95 * (1 - np.exp(-0.15 * x))

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.plot(x, y_random, '--', color=COLORS['grid'], label='Random Sampling', linewidth=2)
ax.plot(x, y_efficient, '-', color=COLORS['BlueLine'], label='Efficient Selection', linewidth=2.5)
ax.fill_between(x, y_random, y_efficient, color=COLORS['BlueL'], alpha=0.1)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.set_xlabel('Dataset Size (% of Total)')
ax.set_ylabel('Model Accuracy (%)')
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)

idx = 40
x_val, y_eff, y_rnd = x[idx], y_efficient[idx], y_random[idx]
ax.annotate("", xy=(x_val, y_eff), xytext=(x_val, y_rnd), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=COLORS['RedLine'], lw=1.0))
ax.text(
    x_val + 0.7,
    y_rnd - 12,
    "Performance Gap\n(Same Data Budget)",
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    fontsize=9,
    va='center',
    fontweight='bold',
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.3),
)

ax.legend(loc='lower right', fontsize=9, frameon=True, facecolor='white', framealpha=0.95, edgecolor='gray', fancybox=True, borderpad=0.6)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

These metrics identify when marginal samples waste training compute rather than improve generalization. They can look good, however, while the reduced set still fails on rare cases, so coverage must be checked as well.

Data selection techniques implicitly rank sample value, and validating that a curated dataset preserves model quality requires systematic benchmarking across three dimensions. Coverage metrics validate that coreset selection preserved representation across classes and demographic groups. Distribution alignment metrics (such as KL divergence and population stability index, which @sec-appdx-data-foundations-measuring-drift-divergence-a6dd defines) detect whether the curated training set drifted from the deployment distribution. Label quality metrics (inter-annotator agreement, and confident learning, which flags examples whose given label disagrees with a model's confident out-of-sample prediction) validate that active learning did not introduce systematic labeling errors. A 50 percent dataset reduction is only valuable if benchmarking confirms the model maintains target accuracy, calibration, and robustness.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Coverage, label-quality, and distribution-alignment checks are developed into a full data-benchmarking protocol in @sec-benchmarking-data-benchmarking-22f9.
:::

The validation target can itself be unreliable. Benchmark accuracy can overstate generalization when test sets fail to capture operational distribution shifts, demanding the same scrutiny for evaluation benchmarks as for curated training sets.

::: {#exmp-data-selection-benchmark-replication-gap .callout-example title="The benchmark replication gap"}

**Scenario**: Classifiers evaluated on newly collected test sets experienced 3 to 15 percentage-point accuracy drops on CIFAR-10 and 11 to 14 points on ImageNet [@recht2019imagenet].

**Diagnosis**: The replicated collection produced slightly harder images than the original test sets. The study found that benchmark adaptivity did not explain the gap, even though repeated use of a fixed test set remains a general evaluation risk.

**Systems lesson**: Evaluation-set construction affects measured generalization. Data-selection pipelines should validate curated subsets on independently collected and deployment-relevant test sets rather than trusting one long-reused benchmark.

:::

An efficiency gain measured against a single benchmark can evaporate under distribution shift; a curated subset must demonstrate consistent quality across multiple held-out distributions before its reported reduction ratio is trusted.

### The selection inequality {#sec-data-selection-selection-inequality-3b7e}

Every measure so far counts learning against training compute alone. A selection method also spends time choosing, and a claim that it shortens training must count that time.

To reduce overall training time at a fixed quality target, selection plus subset training must take less time than training on the full corpus. Let $\SelectionTime$ be total wall-clock selection overhead, including candidate scoring and any prerequisite scorer preparation charged to the training run. Let $\TrainingTime(\DatasetSize)$ be wall-clock training time for a dataset of size $\DatasetSize$, and let $\SubsetDatasetSize$ and $\FullDatasetSize$ be the retained and full sample counts. @Eq-selection-inequality formalizes this break-even condition as the **selection inequality**\index{Selection inequality!definition}:
$$ \SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize) $$ {#eq-selection-inequality}

Equivalently, isolating the allowable selection overhead yields $\SelectionTime< \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize) - \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize)$. The upper bound on selection latency depends strictly on how much training execution the subset eliminates; no arbitrary overhead fraction applies across workloads. When an engineering pipeline can amortize scorer preparation or checkpoint extraction across multiple downstream training runs (@sec-data-selection-amortization-across-training-runs-f6b8), $\SelectionTime$ reflects only the marginal scoring pass over the candidate pool. Conversely, if an auxiliary proxy must be trained from scratch for a single isolated run, that preparatory compute adds directly to $\SelectionTime$. When $\SelectionScoreFunction(\ModelInput)$ repeatedly evaluates the candidate pool using the primary model architecture, recurring scoring passes and distributed coordination can consume the saved training cycles, turning data selection into a net throughput penalty.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: selection-inequality-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTION INEQUALITY WORKED EXAMPLE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Selection inequality in practice" callout; the rescoring estimate
# │          in @sec-data-selection-selection-bottleneck-4d00; the decision
# │          process in @sec-data-selection-decision-process-7a2d.
# │ Scope: chapter-anchor — the final decision reuses the same cost scenario.
# │
# │ Goal: Demonstrate the selection inequality on ResNet-50 and ImageNet.
# │ Show: Both scorers save training time; the proxy reduces only the scoring term.
# │ How: Registry FLOPs for ResNet-50 and ResNet-18, ImageNet size, and one H100
# │      at the reference MFU; scoring is one forward pass over the pool.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, Datasets
from mlsysim.engine import calibration
from mlsysim.core.units import count, second, minute
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt, check, fmt_count, fmt_time

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class SelectionInequalityCalc:
    """Compare one-time target-model and proxy scoring at a fixed retained fraction."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    target = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    proxy = Models.Vision.ResNet18
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    # Same inputs as the training chapter's ResNetFeedH100: sustained fraction implied by
    # 3,000 img/s of training on an A100 (anchor shared with the data engineering chapter)
    a100 = Hardware.Cloud.A100
    a100_sustained_img_s = 3000
    mfu = (a100_sustained_img_s * 3 * Models.Vision.ResNet50.inference_flops.to(flop).magnitude) / a100.compute.peak_flops.to(flop / second).magnitude
    image_count = Datasets.ImageNet.training_examples.to(count)
    coreset_fraction_value = 0.10  # scenario assumption: 10% coreset
    training_epoch_count = 100  # scenario assumption: training epochs

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    rate = h100.compute.peak_flops * mfu
    score_a_time = (image_count.magnitude * target.inference_flops / rate).to(second)
    score_b_time = (image_count.magnitude * proxy.inference_flops / rate).to(second)
    baseline_time = (image_count.magnitude * training_epoch_count * 3 * target.inference_flops / rate).to(second)
    train_a_time = coreset_fraction_value * baseline_time
    total_a_time = score_a_time + train_a_time
    total_b_time = score_b_time + train_a_time
    savings_a_time = baseline_time - total_a_time
    savings_a_fraction = (savings_a_time / baseline_time).to("").magnitude
    savings_b_time = baseline_time - total_b_time
    savings_b_fraction = (savings_b_time / baseline_time).to("").magnitude
    b_beats_a_time = total_a_time - total_b_time
    coreset_image_count = round(image_count.magnitude * coreset_fraction_value)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(savings_b_fraction > savings_a_fraction, "Proxy selection must outperform full-model selection.")
    check(220 < baseline_time.to(minute).magnitude < 230, f"Expected about 225 minutes at the compute-bound rate, got {baseline_time.to(minute)}.")
    check(abs(score_a_time / (baseline_time / training_epoch_count) - 1 / 3) < 1e-9, "Prose says one scoring pass is a third of a full epoch.")
    check(20 < b_beats_a_time.magnitude < 30, f"Expected the proxy to save about 25 seconds, got {b_beats_a_time}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    score_a_s_str = fmt_time(round(score_a_time.magnitude) * second, 'second', precision=0, style='word')
    score_b_s_str = fmt_time(round(score_b_time.magnitude) * second, 'second', precision=0, style='word')
    total_a_min_str = fmt_time(total_a_time, 'minute', precision=1, style='word')
    total_b_min_str = fmt_time(total_b_time, 'minute', precision=1, style='word')
    baseline_min_str = fmt_time(round(baseline_time.to(minute).magnitude) * minute, 'minute', precision=0, style='word')
    baseline_min_attr_str = fmt_time(round(baseline_time.to(minute).magnitude) * minute, 'minute', precision=0, style='word', attributive=True)
    savings_a_min_str = fmt_time(savings_a_time, 'minute', precision=1, style='word')
    savings_a_pct_str = fmt_percent(savings_a_fraction, precision=1, style='prose')
    savings_b_min_str = fmt_time(savings_b_time, 'minute', precision=1, style='word')
    savings_b_pct_str = fmt_percent(savings_b_fraction, precision=1, style='prose')
    b_beats_a_s_str = fmt_time(round(b_beats_a_time.magnitude) * second, 'second', precision=0, style='word')
    n_images_str = fmt_count(image_count, scale='M', precision=2, scale_style='word')
    n_coreset_str = fmt_count(coreset_image_count, precision=0, commas=True)
    n_epochs_str = fmt(training_epoch_count, precision=0, commas=False)
    coreset_pct_str = fmt_percent(coreset_fraction_value, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    mfu_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(mfu, 2), precision=0, style='prose')
```

::: {#exmp-data-selection-selection-inequality-practice .callout-example title="Selection inequality in practice"}

**Scenario**: A computer vision team selects a `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.n_coreset_str`-image coreset (`{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.coreset_pct_str`) from the `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.n_images_str` ImageNet training images to shorten ResNet-50 training on one H100 sustaining `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.mfu_pct_str` of its peak, the training chapter's compute-bound rate. Pretrained checkpoints for both the target architecture and a lightweight proxy are already available from earlier exploration, so this comparison accounts only for a marginal scoring pass over the candidate pool.

**Diagnosis**: Against a `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.baseline_min_attr_str` full-data run of `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.n_epochs_str` epochs, marginal full-model scoring (Option A: target ResNet-50) adds `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.score_a_s_str` of selection overhead and still saves `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.savings_a_min_str` (`{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.savings_a_pct_str`). Marginal proxy-model scoring (Option B: ResNet-18) drops selection overhead to `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.score_b_s_str` and saves `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.savings_b_min_str` (`{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.savings_b_pct_str`), only `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.b_beats_a_s_str` more.

**Systems lesson**: Both options satisfy the selection inequality by a wide margin, because a single scoring pass costs at most one forward pass over the dataset (one-third of a full-data epoch for the target ResNet-50) and less with the proxy, while training on the `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.coreset_pct_str` coreset shrinks every one of the `{python} SelectionInequalityCalc.n_epochs_str` epochs. Scorer choice also becomes decisive when selection rescores dynamically every epoch or when the scoring architecture is significantly larger than the target, multiplying selection latency while subset training savings remain fixed.

:::

End-to-end wall-clock time divides into selection overhead and subset training, and the split decides the outcome across three regimes (@fig-selection-inequality): lightweight proxy scoring limits selection overhead to 5 percent while training on the 40 percent subset (yielding 55 percent net savings), whereas heavyweight scoring expends 60 percent overhead on selection, wiping out all subset-training efficiency gains.

::: {#fig-selection-inequality fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Selection Inequality**: In this illustrative example, data selection only improves end-to-end training time at matched quality if the overhead of selection plus training on the subset is less than training on the full dataset. A lightweight selection function (proxy model, cached embeddings) keeps selection overhead low; an expensive selection function (full model forward pass) can negate the savings." fig-alt="Stacked bar chart comparing three approaches: Baseline shows a single tall bar (100) for full training; Efficient Selection shows two short stacked bars (5 selection overhead plus 40 subset training) totaling 45 with a 55 percent savings annotation; Expensive Selection shows two stacked bars (60 selection overhead plus 40 subset training) totaling 100 with a No savings annotation."}

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTION INEQUALITY FIGURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-selection-inequality (Selection Bottleneck section)
# │
# │ Goal: Visualize the total training cost components under selection.
# │ How: Plot stacked bars for baseline, efficient, and expensive selection scenarios.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Visualize the total training cost components under selection.
import numpy as np
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 3.8))

# —Plot: Selection Inequality Stacked Bars ---

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Scenario assumption (illustrative, per the caption): relative cost units with
# full training = 100; the subset trains at 40 and selection costs 5 or 60.
categories = ['Baseline', 'Efficient Selection', 'Expensive Selection']
full_train_cost = np.array([100, 0, 0])
selection_overhead = np.array([0, 5, 60])
subset_train_cost = np.array([0, 40, 40])
efficient_total = selection_overhead[1] + subset_train_cost[1]
savings_pct = 100 * (1 - efficient_total / full_train_cost[0])

x = np.arange(len(categories))
width = 0.3

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
p1 = ax.bar(x, full_train_cost, width, label='Full Training', color=COLORS['BlueFill'], edgecolor=COLORS['BlueLine'])
p2 = ax.bar(x, selection_overhead, width, bottom=full_train_cost, label='Selection Overhead', color=COLORS['OrangeL'], edgecolor=COLORS['OrangeLine'])
p3 = ax.bar(
    x,
    subset_train_cost,
    width,
    bottom=full_train_cost + selection_overhead,
    label='Subset Training',
    color=COLORS['GreenFill'],
    edgecolor=COLORS['GreenLine'],
)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ax.set_ylabel('Total Time (Normalized)')
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(categories)
ax.set_ylim(0, 117)
# ax.legend(loc='upper right', ncol=3, fontsize=9)
ax.legend(
    loc='lower center',
    bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.01),
    ncol=3,
    fontsize=9,
    frameon=True,
    facecolor='white',
    framealpha=0.95,
    edgecolor='gray',
    fancybox=True,
    borderpad=0.6,
)
ax.annotate("", xy=(1, efficient_total), xytext=(1, full_train_cost[0]), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=COLORS['GreenLine'], lw=1))
ax.text(
    1.05,
    (efficient_total + full_train_cost[0]) / 2,
    f"{savings_pct:.0f}% Savings",
    color=COLORS['GreenLine'],
    fontweight='bold',
    fontsize=9,
    va='center',
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
)
ax.annotate("", xy=(1.85, 100), xytext=(0.15, 100), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", linestyle="--", color=COLORS['grid']))
ax.text(
    2,
    103,
    "No Savings!",
    color=COLORS['RedLine'],
    fontweight='bold',
    fontsize=9,
    ha='center',
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', alpha=0.8, edgecolor='none', pad=0.5),
```
