:::

Tracing artifacts through the pipeline in @fig-optimization-stack shows why data selection sits at the head of the optimization stack: pruning raw inputs reduces upstream training FLOPs, but does not automatically shrink parameter footprint, improve quantization headroom, or relax serving latency constraints in the downstream compression and hardware stages. Each downstream tier inherits both the computational savings and any representational deficits created upstream; an aggressive filter that discards rare but critical edge cases can force downstream engineers to train longer or abandon aggressive quantization to preserve task accuracy. The failure modes that follow show how data selection breaks down in production.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-data-selection-fallacies-pitfalls-f4d0}

Data selection involves counterintuitive diminishing returns that contradict the "more is better" intuition from traditional machine learning. The following errors fall into three groups: conceptual fallacies about what data selection can achieve, implementation pitfalls that arise when correct strategies meet engineering realities, and transfer errors that occur when benchmark results are applied uncritically to new domains.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-fallacy-calc

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FALLACIES CALCULATIONS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Fallacies and Pitfalls section — fallacy prose below
# │
# │ Goal: Quantitative backing for data-selection fallacies.
# │ Show: Diminishing returns, synthetic collapse, scale ROI, benchmark transfer.
# │ How: Pre-compute comparative stats for accuracy and cost scenarios.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import USD, count
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_percent, fmt, fmt_pp, check, fmt_count, fmt_usd

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class FpFallacyCalc:
    """Quantitative backing for Fallacies in the F&P section."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    data_1m_count = 1_000_000 * count
    data_10m_count = 10_000_000 * count
    acc_gain_10x_pp = 4.0
    curated_sample_count = 100_000 * count
    raw_sample_count = 1_000_000 * count
    curated_accuracy_pct = 92.0
    raw_accuracy_pct = 88.0
    synthetic_gen1_acc_pct = 95.0
    synthetic_gen5_acc_pct = 78.0
    training_run_cost = 100_000_000 * USD  # scenario assumption: large-scale training run
    efficiency_gain_pct_value = 10
    cifar10_coreset_pct_value = 50
    cifar10_acc_retained_pct = 98
    imagenet_acc_retained_pct = 95
    medical_acc_retained_pct = 72

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    curated_cost_ratio_value = (raw_sample_count / curated_sample_count).to("").magnitude
    data_scale_value = (data_10m_count / data_1m_count).to("").magnitude
    synthetic_acc_drop_pp = synthetic_gen1_acc_pct - synthetic_gen5_acc_pct
    savings = training_run_cost * efficiency_gain_pct_value / 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(curated_accuracy_pct > raw_accuracy_pct, "Curated small dataset must outperform raw large dataset.")
    check(abs(synthetic_acc_drop_pp - 17.0) < 0.1, f"Expected 17 pp accuracy drop, got {synthetic_acc_drop_pp}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    data_1m_str = fmt_count(data_1m_count, scale='M')
    data_10m_str = fmt_count(data_10m_count, scale='M')
    acc_gain_10x_str = fmt_pp(acc_gain_10x_pp, precision=0)
    synthetic_gen1_acc_str = fmt_percent(synthetic_gen1_acc_pct / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    synthetic_gen5_acc_str = fmt_percent(synthetic_gen5_acc_pct / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    synthetic_acc_drop_pp_str = fmt_pp(synthetic_acc_drop_pp, precision=0, commas=False, attributive=True)
    training_run_cost_str = fmt_usd(training_run_cost, precision=0, commas=False, scale='M')
    efficiency_gain_pct_str = fmt_percent(efficiency_gain_pct_value / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    savings_str = fmt_usd(savings, precision=0, commas=False, scale='M')
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *More data always improves the model enough to justify its cost.*

More data does not imply proportional accuracy gains because learning curves exhibit power-law diminishing returns. Test loss diminishes sub-linearly with dataset size ($\LossFunction(\DatasetSize) \propto \DataScalingLossFactor$ for a fitted exponent $\DataScalingExponent$), meaning each successive error reduction demands a multiplicatively larger corpus. In an illustrative learning-curve scenario, scaling a dataset tenfold from `{python} FpFallacyCalc.data_1m_str` to `{python} FpFallacyCalc.data_10m_str` samples yields only `{python} FpFallacyCalc.acc_gain_10x_str` of accuracy gain. That 10$\times$ volume expansion still costs a tenfold increase in storage I/O, host-to-device transfers, and accelerator FLOPs. Teams should measure the learning curve of their own workload rather than assume that more data delivers proportional value.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Replacing real-data validation with synthetic-only training data.*

Synthetic samples cost almost nothing to acquire, so generative models can look like a replacement for data collection. Synthetic-only training fails in two ways. First, synthetic data can differ from the deployment distribution (@sec-data-selection-bridging-domain-gap-100b, @fig-domain-gap), so the model learns features that fail to transfer; only real-data labels reveal the effect. Second, recursive training on model-generated data can trigger model collapse [@shumailov2024], which progressively erodes distribution tails: in this scenario, evaluation accuracy degrades from `{python} FpFallacyCalc.synthetic_gen1_acc_str` to `{python} FpFallacyCalc.synthetic_gen5_acc_str` across five recursive generations, suffering a `{python} FpFallacyCalc.synthetic_acc_drop_pp_str` collapse. Synthetic mixtures must therefore be validated against curated real data.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
```{=latex}
\vspace*{-20mm}
```
![](images/svg/vol1_data_selection_margin_004.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A single red line falls from 95 percent accuracy at generation 1 to 78 percent at generation 5, a 17-percentage-point decline."}

*Illustrative model collapse: accuracy erodes with each recursive synthetic generation.*
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Data selection is merely data cleaning.*

A dataset can be completely clean and correctly labeled yet redundant: once the model has minimized loss on a feature cluster, further identical samples add almost no gradient signal and still consume memory bandwidth and accelerator FLOPs. Cleaning corrects intrinsic defects; selection raises the learning return per FLOP by choosing examples for task-relevant information and coverage (@fig-coreset-selection; @sec-data-selection-coreset-selection-algorithms-2c74). In the worked coreset scenario of notebook \ref{nbk-data-selection-computing-icr-coresets}, the selected subset reached `{python} IcrCoresetComparison.icr_ratio_mult_str` higher ICR.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating data selection as a budget-only tactic.*

Selection can look like a technique for resource-constrained teams, as if frontier foundation models could brute-force convergence by scaling the cluster. The data wall binds at every scale. At frontier scale, token consumption converges toward the finite ceiling of high-quality human text (@fig-running-out-of-human-data); at GPT-2 scale, one eight-H100 machine passes over the whole WebText corpus about `{python} GPT2DataWall.corpus_passes_str` times in `{python} GPT2DataWall.node_days_str` (@sec-data-selection-data-selection-fundamentals-e839). The economic return of selection also scales with cluster expenditure: a `{python} FpFallacyCalc.efficiency_gain_pct_str` efficiency gain on a `{python} FpFallacyCalc.training_run_cost_str` frontier training run saves `{python} FpFallacyCalc.savings_str` under these assumptions. Amortizing scores and cached embeddings across repeated runs (@sec-data-selection-amortization-across-training-runs-f6b8) strengthens the case further.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fp-pitfall-calc

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PITFALLS CALCULATIONS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Fallacies and Pitfalls section — pitfall prose below
# │
# │ Goal: Quantitative backing for data-selection implementation pitfalls.
# │ Show: Selection overhead, rare-class pruning, AL latency, metric mismatch.
# │ How: Pre-compute timing, sampling, and accuracy scenarios.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent, fmt_count, fmt_time

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class FpPitfallCalc:
    """Quantitative backing for Pitfalls in the F&P section."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    selection_time_bad = 10 * hour  # scenario assumption: expensive selection
    training_time = 2 * hour  # scenario assumption: subset training run
    full_training_time = 8 * hour  # scenario assumption: full training run
    selection_time_good = 0.5 * hour  # scenario assumption: proxy scoring
    total_sample_count = 1_000_000 * count
    rare_class_pct_value = 0.1
    coreset_pct_value = 10
    min_sample_threshold = 150 * count
    al_latency = 14 * day  # scenario assumption: annotation turnaround
    model_drift_epoch_count = 10
    batch_size_small_count = 100
    batch_size_large_count = 1000
    coreset_size_pct_value = 10
    rare_class_acc_pct = 45
    majority_class_acc_pct = 97

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    selection_overhead_ratio_value = (selection_time_bad / training_time).to("").magnitude
    selection_overhead_good_fraction = selection_time_good / full_training_time
    rare_class_count = total_sample_count * rare_class_pct_value / 100
    expected_rare_in_coreset = rare_class_count * coreset_pct_value / 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(expected_rare_in_coreset < min_sample_threshold, "Random coreset should drop rare class below minimum threshold.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    selection_time_bad_hours_str = fmt_time(selection_time_bad, 'hour', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    training_time_hours_str = fmt_time(
        training_time,
        "hour",
        precision=0,
        commas=False,
        style="word",
    )
    selection_overhead_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(selection_overhead_ratio_value), precision=0, commas=False)
    selection_time_good_min_str = fmt_time(selection_time_good, 'minute', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    selection_overhead_good_pct_str = fmt_percent(selection_overhead_good_fraction, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    full_training_time_hours_str = fmt_time(full_training_time, 'hour', precision=0, commas=False, style='word')
    total_samples_str = fmt_count(total_sample_count, scale='M')
    rare_class_pct_str = fmt_percent(rare_class_pct_value / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    rare_class_count_str = fmt_count(rare_class_count, precision=0, commas=True)
    fp_coreset_pct_str = fmt_percent(coreset_pct_value / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    expected_rare_in_coreset_str = fmt_count(expected_rare_in_coreset, precision=0, commas=False)
    min_samples_threshold_str = fmt_count(min_sample_threshold, precision=0, commas=False)
    al_latency_days_str = fmt_time(al_latency, 'day', precision=0, commas=False, style='word', attributive=True)
    coreset_size_pct_str = fmt_percent(coreset_size_pct_value / 100, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Selection overhead is too small to change training economics.*

The selection inequality (@eq-selection-inequality) requires $\SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize)$ at matched quality. Consider a baseline training run requiring `{python} FpPitfallCalc.full_training_time_hours_str`, where training on an optimized coreset takes `{python} FpPitfallCalc.training_time_hours_str`. If a complex selection algorithm requires `{python} FpPitfallCalc.selection_time_bad_hours_str` to compute sample importance, the selection step alone consumes `{python} FpPitfallCalc.selection_overhead_ratio_mult_str` the duration of the accelerated training run and exceeds the full training baseline itself, a net wall-clock loss. In the illustrative comparison, proxy-based EL2N scoring completes in `{python} FpPitfallCalc.selection_time_good_min_str`, just `{python} FpPitfallCalc.selection_overhead_good_pct_str` of the full-training baseline, which satisfies the inequality.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Pruning rare classes without a coverage floor.*

Standard selection objectives minimize aggregate loss, which gives tail slices little influence over sampling. In a `{python} FpPitfallCalc.total_samples_str` dataset where rare classes comprise `{python} FpPitfallCalc.rare_class_pct_str` of the data (`{python} FpPitfallCalc.rare_class_count_str` examples), an unstratified `{python} FpPitfallCalc.fp_coreset_pct_str` coreset retains only `{python} FpPitfallCalc.expected_rare_in_coreset_str` rare-class examples in expectation, far below the illustrative `{python} FpPitfallCalc.min_samples_threshold_str`-sample retention floor assumed here. An appropriate floor must be validated from task-specific learning curves and critical-slice performance. Importance sampling\index{Importance sampling!gradient variance} can compensate by weighting losses by inverse selection probabilities, but extreme weights inflate gradient variance and force smaller learning rates. As recommended in @sec-data-selection-coreset-selection-algorithms-2c74, production coreset pipelines enforce hard stratification floors per class or critical slice before spending the remaining selection budget.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Deduplicating training data is enough to make evaluation reliable.*

Web-scale pipelines scrape training, validation, and benchmark splits from common crawls, which introduces silent cross-split leakage. When an evaluation set contains near-duplicates of training documents, the metric measures memorization rather than generalization. A deduplication study found that train-test overlap affects over 4 percent of validation examples across standard language-modeling benchmarks [@lee2022]. Deduplicating the training partition alone leaves this contamination untouched; cross-partition deduplication is required, using $\NgramLength$-gram matching or MinHash LSH (@sec-data-selection-data-deduplication-6c20). For a frozen evaluation set, remove the overlapping training records and preserve the evaluation set and its provenance.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Active learning without considering annotation latency.*

Textbook formulations of active learning assume an oracle that labels queries instantly. Production annotation queues introduce delays such as the illustrative `{python} FpPitfallCalc.al_latency_days_str` latency between sample dispatch and label return assumed here. This latency breaks the active learning feedback loop in two ways. If accelerator clusters halt training while awaiting labels, expensive hardware sits idle, destroying cluster compute utilization. Conversely, if training continues asynchronously on background data while annotations are pending, model weights drift across training steps; by the time the labels arrive, the uncertainty scores that justified querying those samples are obsolete. Dispatching large batches to amortize the turnaround adds redundancy within the batch unless diversity penalties are applied.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *If a technique works on ImageNet, it will work on my dataset.*

CIFAR-10 and ImageNet are highly redundant across canonical object classes, which allows coreset pruning of often 30 to 50 percent without measurable accuracy loss. Histopathology, satellite imagery, and industrial defect detection have heavy-tailed feature distributions in which safety-critical patterns appear in a few rare samples. A 50 percent cut tuned on ImageNet can remove the few examples that separate subtle pathologies. Geometric coreset algorithms also depend on embeddings, and a feature extractor pretrained on natural images may not resolve fine-grained domain distinctions. Teams should measure the redundancy of their own data and validate retention across critical slices before pruning.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Optimizing data selection metrics instead of deployment metrics.*

Selection algorithms optimize aggregate surrogates such as area under the learning curve (AULC) or performance-per-data (PPD, @sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9). A selection policy retaining a `{python} FpPitfallCalc.coreset_size_pct_str` coreset can achieve superior aggregate PPD by prioritizing dense clusters of common, easy samples that accelerate average convergence, while discarding ambiguous edge cases and rare slices. Production failures, however, occur on tail slices, edge cases, and protected sub-populations rather than on averages. A policy without subgroup constraints can pass global validation and still fail in deployment. As the measurement framework of @sec-data-selection-measurement-framework-733b requires, policies must be evaluated on stratified, slice-level benchmarks, even when doing so slightly lowers average PPD.

:::

## Summary {#sec-data-selection-summary-cf3e}

Data selection treats training volume as an engineering variable rather than a fixed constraint. Where traditional machine learning asks how many samples reach target accuracy, systems engineering minimizes total cost across compute, storage, labeling, energy, and wall-clock time. Curated datasets can match or outperform massive uncurated corpora because marginal learning signal varies by orders of magnitude across raw examples.

This systems perspective becomes actionable through three quantitative tools: the ICR, the selection inequality, and the total data cost model. The information-compute ratio quantifies learning gained per floating-point operation, providing a proxy for sample value that must be evaluated alongside coverage and target quality. The selection inequality tests a training-time claim by requiring scoring plus subset training to take less time than full-data training at matched quality. Together with return-on-investment and break-even analysis, these formulations determine whether a proposed selection mechanism saves resources or merely shifts expenditure between stages.

The three levers act at different points: static pruning removes redundancy before training, dynamic selection prioritizes informative examples during training, and synthetic generation creates data where none exists. Together, these levers answer the data wall, the gap between rapidly growing compute capacity and slowly growing high-quality data.

Learning from unlabeled data sits beside these levers rather than within them. Semi-supervised learning stretches a small labeled seed across an unlabeled pool, and self-supervised pretraining moves the bulk of representation learning into an unannotated upstream phase, so downstream tasks can reach target quality with far fewer task-specific labels; the worked amortization scenario assumes `{python} FoundationCostAmortization.label_cost_reduction_factor_mult_str` fewer. The compute-only crossover occurs at roughly `{python} FoundationCostAmortization.crossover_tasks_str` tasks under the scenario assumptions. Labeling savings enter a separate dollar comparison that also requires compute prices and other differing costs.

In production, the difficult part is rarely the scoring rule itself. It is keeping selection from becoming the next bottleneck. Proxy models and cached embeddings bound scoring time, shard-based loaders keep storage access sequential, and data echoing recovers accelerator cycles when ingestion lags. On one H100, a half-size ResNet-50 coreset saves about `{python} ResNetEpochOnH100.pruned_time_str` and `{python} ResNetEpochOnH100.pruned_energy_str` per epoch against a one-time scoring pass of about `{python} ResNetEpochOnH100.score_time_str`, and those seconds are realized only when the host keeps the accelerator fed. Controlled model-size and data sweeps diagnose whether a run is data-limited or compute-limited in the first place, and PPD, AULC, and DCR then show whether a reduction delivered what it promised at the binding resource.

Every row of the opening chapter map (@tbl-data-selection-chapter-spine) has now been derived, and the formulas behind its tests fit on one page (@tbl-data-selection-key-equations). Together they let an engineer estimate, before committing a training run, whether a lever saves more than it costs.

| **Quantity**                       | **Formula**                                                                                                                           | **Where derived**                                                       |
|:-----------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Information-compute ratio**      | $\text{ICR} = \FiniteChange\DataInformationContent/\FiniteChange\Operations$                                                          | @sec-data-selection-informationcompute-ratio-8c0b                       |
| **Marginal ICR (log-information)** | $\text{ICR}(\DatasetSize) \approx 1/(\OperationsPerSample\cdot \DatasetSize)$                                                         | @eq-icr-decay                                                           |
| **Performance-per-data**           | $\text{PPD}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) = [\text{Accuracy}(\LearningCurveSampleCount) - \text{Accuracy}(0)]/\LearningCurveSampleCount$ | @sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9                                   |
| **Data compression ratio**         | $\text{DCR} = \FullDatasetSize/\SubsetDatasetSize$ at target accuracy                                                                 | @sec-data-selection-core-metrics-32e9                                   |
| **Training compute**               | $\Operations \approx 6\Parameters\DatasetSize$; compute-optimal tokens $\ComputeOptimalTokenCount \propto \sqrt{\Operations}$         | @sec-data-selection-computeoptimal-frontier-24ba                        |
| **Selection inequality**           | $\SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize)$                                                 | @eq-selection-inequality                                                |
| **Curriculum warmup samples**      | $\DatasetSize (\WarmupEpochCount+1)/2$ in place of $\WarmupEpochCount\cdot \DatasetSize$                                              | @sec-data-selection-curriculum-learning-easy-hard-2c4e                  |
| **Offline distillation targets**   | $4\ClassCount$ bytes per sample in place of $\lceil \log_2 \ClassCount \rceil$ bits                                                   | @sec-data-selection-knowledge-distillation-compressing-information-ce68 |
| **Input-pipeline ratio**           | $\InputPipelineRatio= \HostPreparationTime/\AcceleratorBatchTime$; echoing helps up to $\EchoFactor= \InputPipelineRatio$             | @sec-data-selection-data-echoing-amortizing-io-costs-b4e0               |
| **Total cost of data**             | $\TotalDataCost= \DataAcquisitionCost+ \DataLabelingCost+ \DataStorageCost+ \DataProcessingCost$                                      | @sec-data-selection-quantifying-data-costs-roi-f0b4                     |
| **Amortized return on investment** | Savings across $\TrainingRunCount$ runs, less the one-time investment, per unit invested                                              | @eq-data-selection-amortized-roi                                        |

: **Key Equations**: The chapter's counting rules in the notation of the sections that derive them. The training-compute rule is the dense-transformer accounting of the GPT-2 lighthouse; the curriculum rule assumes linear pacing over $\WarmupEpochCount$ warmup epochs. {#tbl-data-selection-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[24,52,24]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Curate, do not accumulate"}

* **Selection optimizes system cost**: The objective is minimizing total cost across compute, storage, labeling, and energy rather than reducing sample counts alone. The information-compute ratio measures learning gained per FLOP spent; total-cost accounting and pipeline measurements establish whether that gain serves the system objective.
* **Start with deduplication**: Exact deduplication is often the lowest-risk first technique because it removes repeated bytes without a learned scoring pass. Apply near-duplicate and semantic deduplication only after validating thresholds against downstream quality metrics.
* **Training-time savings must exceed selection overhead**: At matched quality, $\SelectionTime+ \TrainingTime(\SubsetDatasetSize) < \TrainingTime(\FullDatasetSize)$. Lightweight proxy models and cached embeddings keep $\SelectionTime$ low, whereas unoptimized selection algorithms can consume all the compute they save.
* **Dynamic selection adapts the training mix**: Curriculum learning changes presentation order, while active learning changes which samples receive labels. Either improves efficiency when its scoring rule, coverage, and refresh overhead are validated.
* **Self-supervised pretraining can amortize adaptation cost**: Pretraining once and fine-tuning many times spreads pretraining cost across downstream tasks. The worked scenario assumes a `{python} FoundationCostAmortization.label_cost_reduction_factor_mult_str` label reduction and a `{python} FoundationCostAmortization.marginal_compute_reduction_mult_str` marginal-compute reduction; realized savings depend on transfer quality and reuse.
* **Synthetic data is a supplement, not a replacement**: Synthetic samples augment scarce tail cases effectively, but cannot substitute entirely for empirical data. Unanchored synthetic training introduces domain-gap degradation, and recursive synthetic loops trigger catastrophic model collapse.
* **Validated workload reduction compounds downstream**: When selection safely eliminates examples or tokens without adding compensating steps, that work never reaches later model or machine optimizations. Dynamic scoring and synthesis add their own costs, so the combined saving must be measured rather than assumed.

:::

Examples differ greatly in how much they teach per byte transferred and per FLOP executed, and selection spends compute on the ones that teach most. Within the D·A·M taxonomy, selection operates at the head of the system: every redundant sample or uninformative token safely eliminated directly reduces operation count ($\Operations$) in the iron law of ML systems (principle \ref{pri-iron-law}) and can avoid downstream training reads. Scoring may still read the entire pool, and shard streaming may read discarded records, so reductions in data volume ($\DataVolume$) must count scoring and shard-read traffic separately. When selection overhead satisfies the inequality at matched quality, the reduction removes work before downstream compression or hardware acceleration sees it. Model-based scoring offers a way to invest additional compute in selection, consistent with the bitter lesson, but a stronger scorer justifies that investment only if its improved rankings save more downstream work than it costs. The Pareto frontier (principle \ref{pri-pareto-frontier}) applies upstream of the model as well. Each retained fraction is an operating point that trades coverage and rare-slice accuracy against compute, and no single fraction is optimal for every workload.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From data to algorithms"}

Data selection changes *what* the system learns from. @Sec-model-compression turns to *how* the model represents what it has learned. It starts from the deployment envelope the model must fit and adjusts three things to fit it: the model's structure through pruning and distillation, its numerical precision through quantization, and the way the remaining operations map onto the hardware that executes them.
